---
title: "Two Rankings from One Posterior: A Bayesian Power Rating and a Wins-Above-Benchmark Resume for College Football"
abstract: "A college football ranking is asked two questions: which team is better, and which has earned more. The first is predictive and should use margin of victory; the second is retrodictive and should reward only results. We answer both from one Bayesian model. Team strength, in points on a neutral field, is observed through the regulation margin and an efficiency margin built from expected points added, modelled jointly so that one performance is not counted twice, pooled within conferences and divisional tiers, carried over between seasons with roster information, and allowed to drift from week to week as a random walk. The shape of the margin distribution is chosen among four families by leave-one-out cross-validation, and a parallel model for the total score splits strength into offence and defence. The power rating is the posterior of strength. The resume, Wins Above Benchmark, counts the wins a team has beyond those the twelfth-best team would expect against the same schedule, computed per posterior draw. We evaluate the system on every week of every season since 2014 with convergence gates, posterior predictive and prior-sensitivity checks, simulation-based calibration, ablations, and a rolling out-of-sample backtest against results, closing betting lines and totals, and baseline ratings."
date: last-modified

```{r, setup}
#| include: false
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE,
  echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%",
  dev = "cairo_pdf", dpi = 300
)

# Rendered with execute-dir: project (see _quarto.yml), so the working
# directory is normally the project root; fall back to the parent otherwise.
root <- if (file.exists("_targets.R")) "." else ".."
store <- file.path(root, "_targets")

# Colour encodes the product and nothing else: Power in orange, Resume in blue,
# the betting market and every reference in grey. Emphasis is weight, not hue.
col_power <- "#D1622A"
col_resume <- "#3A6EA5"
col_ink <- "#202020"
col_ref <- "gray55"
col_faint <- "gray85"

theme_paper <- function(base_size = 10) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "gray92", linewidth = 0.3),
      axis.title = element_text(colour = "gray30"),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = "gray30"),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0, colour = col_ink),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = element_blank(),
      plot.title.position = "plot"
    )
}
theme_set(theme_paper())

fmt <- function(v, d = 0) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
# Inside $...$ a bare comma is punctuation; {,} typesets a digit separator.
fmtm <- function(v, d = 0) gsub(",", "{,}", fmt(v, d), fixed = TRUE)
pct <- function(v, d = 0) paste0(fmt(100 * v, d), "\\%")
ktab <- function(df, ...) {
  kable(df, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", escape = FALSE, ...)
}
```

```{r, data}
# Literal target names, so that tar_quarto() registers each as a dependency
cfg <- targets::tar_read(cfg, store = store)
snapshots <- targets::tar_read(snapshots, store = store)
params <- snapshots$params
ratings <- targets::tar_read(ratings, store = store)
bt <- targets::tar_read(backtest, store = store)
games <- targets::tar_read(games_all, store = store)
checks <- Filter(Negate(is.null), targets::tar_read(checks, store = store))
refits <- targets::tar_read(prior_refits, store = store)
last_full <- targets::tar_read(last_full, store = store)
struct <- refits
# The published priors are pool_priors(refits, pool = cfg$pool) (R/07_analysis.R): recency-weighted
# means of the full-season posterior means under vague priors, 2014 left out (and 2020 for home
# field), with the random-effects predictive sd for a new season.
pooled <- targets::tar_read(pooled_priors, store = store)

seasons <- sort(unique(params$season))
first_season <- min(seasons)
current <- max(seasons)
# Complete seasons: those whose postseason is over (the same rule as the pipeline's LAST_FULL)
complete <- seasons[seasons <= last_full]

final <- params |> group_by(season) |> filter(week == max(week)) |> ungroup()
final_full <- final |> filter(season %in% complete)

n_snap <- nrow(params)
n_pass <- sum(params$passed)
n_retry <- sum(params$attempts > 1)
n_games_all <- sum(games$completed, na.rm = TRUE)

ov <- bt$overall
bt_all <- ov |> filter(scope == "All games")
bt_fbs <- ov |> filter(scope == "FBS vs FBS")
bt_late <- ov |> filter(scope == "FBS vs FBS, week 5+")

# The Gaussian information calculation of @sec-info, at each complete season's
# final posterior mean.
info <- final_full |>
  transmute(
    season, lambda, kappa, sigma_eff, sigma_m, nu,
    S11 = sigma_eff^2, S12 = kappa * sigma_eff^2, S22 = sigma_m^2 + kappa^2 * sigma_eff^2,
    i_y = 1 / S22,
    i_joint = lambda^2 / sigma_eff^2 + (1 - kappa * lambda)^2 / sigma_m^2,
    gain = i_joint / i_y - 1,
    lambda_star = S12 / S22,
    r2 = kappa^2 * sigma_eff^2 / S22
  )

fin_last <- ratings |> filter(season == last_full, tier == 1) |> filter(week == max(week))

# The published margin family (chosen by the margin_comparison target, @sec-family)
fam <- cfg$margin_family
fam_name <- c(normal = "normal", t = "Student-$t$", mixture = "two-normal scale mixture", scale_t = "scale-$t$")
has_nu <- fam %in% c("t", "scale_t")
# Predictive P(margin > 0) at expected margin mu, given posterior-mean family parameters
# (the same laws as margin_cdf() in R/03_rankings.R)
win_plugin <- function(mu, p, family = fam) {
  switch(family,
    normal = pnorm(mu / p$sigma),
    t = pt(mu / p$sigma, p$nu),
    mixture = (1 - p$p_wide) * pnorm(mu / p$sigma) + p$p_wide * pnorm(mu / p$sigma_w),
    scale_t = pt(mu / sqrt(p$sigma^2 + (p$gamma * mu)^2), p$nu))
}
```

```{r, analyses}
# Analyses beyond the published pipeline (R/07_analysis.R)
abl <- targets::tar_read(ablation_scores, store = store)
loso <- targets::tar_read(loso_scores, store = store)
base_sc <- targets::tar_read(baseline_scores, store = store)
ext <- targets::tar_read(external_ratings, store = store)
fr <- targets::tar_read(final_refits, store = store)
leak <- targets::tar_read(margin_leakage, store = store)
sbc <- targets::tar_read(sbc, store = store)
sg <- targets::tar_read(schedule_graph, store = store)
rv <- targets::tar_read(resume_check, store = store)
dh <- targets::tar_read(data_hashes, store = store)
ps2020 <- targets::tar_read(prior_sensitivity_2020, store = store)

# Model checks, for statements made before the checks section
sens_all <- map_dfr(checks, \(x) mutate(x$sensitivity, season = x$season)) |> filter(!is.na(variable))
ppc_all <- map_dfr(checks, \(x) mutate(x$ppc, season = x$season))
w7 <- ppc_all |> filter(statistic == "Share within 7 pts")
n_w7_fail <- sum(w7$observed > w7$rep_hi)
flag_counts <- sens_all |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(conflict = sum(grepl("conflict", diagnosis)), weak = sum(grepl("weak", diagnosis)),
            n = n(), .groups = "drop")
n_flagged_any <- sum(flag_counts$conflict + flag_counts$weak > 0)

# Paired comparison of two sets of game scores with season-week cluster standard errors
paired <- function(a, b, metric) {
  j <- inner_join(a |> select(season, game_id, week_seq, x = all_of(metric)),
                  b |> select(season, game_id, y = all_of(metric)), by = c("season", "game_id"))
  d <- j$x - j$y
  u <- tapply(d - mean(d), paste(j$season, j$week_seq), sum)
  c(diff = mean(d), se = sqrt(sum(u^2)) / length(d), n = length(d))
}
score_sum <- function(df) {
  df |> summarise(games = n(), mae = mean(abs(err)), rmse = sqrt(mean(err^2)), brier = mean(brier),
                  logloss = mean(logloss), crps = if ("crps" %in% names(df)) mean(crps) else NA_real_, .groups = "drop")
}

# Ablations: every variant predicts the same games
abl_seasons <- sort(unique(abl$season))
abl_pub <- abl |> filter(variant == "Published model")
abl_sum <- abl |> group_by(variant) |> score_sum()
abl_diff <- map_dfr(setdiff(unique(abl$variant), "Published model"), function(v) {
  a <- abl |> filter(variant == v)
  bind_rows(lapply(c("err_abs", "brier", "crps"), function(m) {
    aa <- mutate(a, err_abs = abs(err)); bb <- mutate(abl_pub, err_abs = abs(err))
    x <- paired(aa, bb, m)
    tibble(variant = v, metric = m, diff = x[["diff"]], se = x[["se"]])
  }))
})
abl_d <- function(v, m) abl_diff |> filter(variant == v, metric == m)
ablation_order <- c("Published model", "Margin only", "No carry-over", "No conference level", "Static ratings",
                    "Normal margin", "Student-t margin", "Mixture margin", "Scale-t margin")

# Margin families (@sec-family): pooled PSIS-LOO against the Student-t, per season and pooled
mf <- targets::tar_read(margin_families, store = store)
fam_lab <- c(t = "Student-$t$", mixture = "Mixture", scale_t = "Scale-$t$", normal = "Normal")
mf_season <- mf$per_season
mf_pool <- mf_season |>
  group_by(family) |>
  summarise(elpd = sum(elpd), diff = sum(diff), se = sqrt(sum(se^2)), seasons = n(),
            better = sum(diff > 0), better2 = sum(diff > 2 * se), bad_k = sum(n_bad_k),
            passed = all(passed), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(elpd))
mf_best <- mf_pool$family[1]
mf_ppc <- mf$ppc
mf_miss <- mf_ppc |>
  group_by(family, statistic) |>
  summarise(out = sum(observed > rep_hi | observed < rep_lo), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
miss_of <- function(f, s) mf_miss |> filter(family == f, statistic == s)

# Random-walk step sizes by season: published final posterior means
rw_s <- final_full |> select(season, tau, tau_t)

# Margin-only model: LOO of the margin's marginal density at each final posterior
loo_cmp <- map_dfr(fr, function(x) {
  e <- x$loo_compare
  tibble(season = x$season, full = e$elpd_loo[e$model == "full"], margin = e$elpd_loo[e$model == "margin"],
         se = max(e$se_diff))
}) |> mutate(diff = full - margin)

# Baselines and the published model on the same games (from 2015, predicted week 2 on)
pub_games <- bt$games |> transmute(season, game_id, week_seq, err, brier, logloss, fbs_game)
base_cmp <- base_sc |>
  group_by(method) |>
  group_modify(function(df, key) {
    j <- inner_join(df |> select(season, game_id, week_seq, e_b = err, b_b = brier, l_b = logloss, fbs_game),
                    pub_games |> select(season, game_id, e_m = err, b_m = brier, l_m = logloss), by = c("season", "game_id"))
    bind_rows(
      j |> summarise(scope = "All games", games = n(), mae_base = mean(abs(e_b)), mae_model = mean(abs(e_m)),
                     brier_base = mean(b_b), brier_model = mean(b_m)),
      j |> filter(fbs_game) |> summarise(scope = "FBS vs FBS", games = n(), mae_base = mean(abs(e_b)), mae_model = mean(abs(e_m)),
                     brier_base = mean(b_b), brier_model = mean(b_m))
    )
  }) |> ungroup()

# Published SP+ and FPI against the final power rating, FBS teams
ext_cor <- ext |>
  inner_join(ratings |> filter(tier == 1) |> group_by(season) |> filter(week == max(week)) |> ungroup() |>
               select(season, team_id, power), by = c("season", "team_id")) |>
  group_by(system, season) |>
  summarise(rho = cor(rating, power, method = "spearman"), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

# Leave-one-season-out priors in weeks 1-4, against the published predictions of the same games
loso_cmp <- inner_join(loso |> transmute(season, game_id, week_seq, e_l = err, b_l = brier),
                       pub_games |> select(season, game_id, e_m = err, b_m = brier), by = c("season", "game_id"))

sup <- targets::tar_read(supplement, store = store)

# Parameter names as bare symbols, for running text and tables; every structural parameter of
# stan/power.stan, keyed by its name in the fit (model_vars() in R/02_model.R)
sym_lab <- c(hfa = "\\eta", b_prev = "\\beta", lambda = "\\lambda", kappa = "\\kappa",
             sigma_eff = "\\sigma_e", sigma_m = "\\sigma_m", nu = "\\nu", sigma_conf = "\\omega",
             `sigma_team[1]` = "\\tau_1", `sigma_team[2]` = "\\tau_2", `sigma_team[3]` = "\\tau_3",
             `mu_tier[2]` = "m_2", `mu_tier[3]` = "m_3",
             gamma_m = "\\gamma", sigma_w = "\\sigma_w", p_wide = "p_w", tau_r = "\\phi_r",
             `base_raw[1]` = "\\theta", `t_tier_raw[1]` = "m^t_2", `t_tier_raw[2]` = "m^t_3",
             `sigma_conf_t_raw[1]` = "\\omega_t", `sigma_t_team_raw[1]` = "\\tau^t", `b_prev_t_raw[1]` = "\\beta_t",
             `lambda_t_raw[1]` = "\\lambda_t", `alpha_es_raw[1]` = "\\alpha_s", `sigma_es_raw[1]` = "\\sigma_s",
             `kappa_t_raw[1]` = "\\kappa_t", `sigma_tot_raw[1]` = "\\sigma_x", `tau_t_raw[1]` = "\\phi_t",
             `b_ret_raw[1]` = "\\beta_q", `c_ret_raw[1]` = "\\gamma_q", `b_tal_raw[1]` = "\\gamma_a",
             `b_prev2_raw[1]` = "\\beta_2", `b_prev_low_raw[1]` = "\\beta_{\\mathrm{low}}", `delta_coach_raw[1]` = "\\delta_c")
var_tex <- setNames(paste0("$", sym_lab, "$"), names(sym_lab))
# Parameters of the total model (they share nothing with the margin model, @sec-total)
total_vars <- c("base_raw[1]", "t_tier_raw[1]", "t_tier_raw[2]", "sigma_conf_t_raw[1]", "sigma_t_team_raw[1]",
                "b_prev_t_raw[1]", "lambda_t_raw[1]", "alpha_es_raw[1]", "sigma_es_raw[1]", "kappa_t_raw[1]",
                "sigma_tot_raw[1]", "tau_t_raw[1]")
# Preseason terms of @eq-hier
pre_vars <- c("b_ret_raw[1]", "c_ret_raw[1]", "b_tal_raw[1]", "b_prev2_raw[1]", "b_prev_low_raw[1]", "delta_coach_raw[1]")
sym_list <- function(v) {
  s <- paste0("$", sym_lab[v], "$")
  if (length(s) <= 1) return(s)
  paste(paste(s[-length(s)], collapse = ", "), "and", s[length(s)])
}

# Reliability of last season's rating as a covariate
di_rel <- ratings |> filter(tier == 1) |> group_by(season) |> filter(week == max(week)) |>
  summarise(sd_med = median(power_sd), sd_d = sd(power), reliability = 1 - mean(power_sd^2) / var(power),
            .groups = "drop")

# Programmes moving from FCS to FBS, and the early-week error on their games
cls <- bind_rows(games |> transmute(season, team_id = home_id, team = home_team, class = home_class),
                 games |> transmute(season, team_id = away_id, team = away_team, class = away_class)) |>
  filter(!is.na(class)) |> distinct(season, team_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
movers <- cls |>
  inner_join(cls |> transmute(season = season + 1L, team_id, prev_class = class), by = c("season", "team_id")) |>
  filter(class == "fbs", prev_class == "fcs")
mover_key <- paste(movers$season, movers$team_id)
bt_ids <- bt$games |> left_join(games |> select(season, game_id, home_id, away_id), by = c("season", "game_id"))
mover_err <- bt_ids |>
  filter(fbs_game, week_seq <= 4) |>
  mutate(home_m = paste(season, home_id) %in% mover_key, away_m = paste(season, away_id) %in% mover_key,
         mover = home_m | away_m) |>
  group_by(mover) |>
  summarise(games = n(), mae = mean(abs(err)), bias = mean(ifelse(home_m, err, -err)), .groups = "drop")

# Conference means at the end of the last complete season, by tier
conf_sd <- local({
  f <- sup$final
  pm <- posterior::as_draws_df(f$par)
  u <- unclass(posterior::as_draws_matrix(f$conf_raw))
  mt <- cbind(0, pm$`mu_tier[2]`, pm$`mu_tier[3]`)
  alpha <- mt[, f$conf_tier, drop = FALSE] + pm$sigma_conf * u
  tibble(tier = f$conf_tier, alpha = colMeans(alpha)) |> group_by(tier) |> summarise(sd = sd(alpha), n = n())
})

# Home field by season (full-season fits under vague priors)
hfa_s <- refits |> filter(variable == "hfa") |> select(season, mean, sd)

# Final-week refits with every draw: SOR variants, benchmark rank, Monte Carlo errors
sor_cmp <- local({
  x <- map_dfr(fr, \(f) mutate(f$sor, season = f$season))
  per <- x |> group_by(season) |>
    summarise(rho = cor(sor_mean_pi, sor_per_draw, method = "spearman"),
              # the strict version is undefined (NA) for a team that won every game
              rho_s = cor(sor_mean_pi, sor_strict, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"), .groups = "drop")
  list(max_diff = max(abs(x$sor_mean_pi - x$sor_per_draw)), min_rho = min(per$rho), min_rho_strict = min(per$rho_s))
})
bench_cmp <- map_dfr(fr, function(f) {
  b12 <- f$bench |> filter(b == 12L)
  map_dfr(c(4L, 25L), function(k) {
    j <- inner_join(f$bench |> filter(b == k), b12, by = "team_id", suffix = c("", "_12"))
    tibble(season = f$season, b = k, rho = cor(j$wab, j$wab_12, method = "spearman"),
           top12_changes = sum(xor(j$rank <= 12, j$rank_12 <= 12)) / 2,
           top4_changes = sum(xor(j$rank <= 4, j$rank_12 <= 4)) / 2,
           max_move_top25 = max(abs(j$rank - j$rank_12)[j$rank_12 <= 25]))
  })
})
mcse_sum <- map_dfr(fr, \(f) mutate(f$mcse, season = f$season)) |>
  group_by(set, draws) |>
  summarise(across(c(wab, p_top12, rank_q10, rank_q90),
                   list(med = \(x) median(x, na.rm = TRUE), max = \(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE))), .groups = "drop")
mc_thin <- mcse_sum |> filter(set == "thinned"); mc_all <- mcse_sum |> filter(set == "all")

# FBS independents over the period
fbs_ind <- bind_rows(games |> transmute(team = home_team, class = home_class, conf = home_conference),
                     games |> transmute(team = away_team, class = away_class, conf = away_conference)) |>
  filter(class %in% "fbs", is.na(conf) | grepl("Independent", conf)) |>
  count(team, sort = TRUE) |> pull(team)
n_fbs_ind <- length(fbs_ind)

# Schedule graph
sg_final <- sg |> group_by(season) |> filter(week == max(week)) |> ungroup()
sg_first <- sg |> filter(!is.na(fbs_components)) |> group_by(season) |>
  summarise(first_connected = min(week[fbs_components == 1], Inf), .groups = "drop")
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Every autumn, some one hundred and thirty teams in the Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS) play about twelve games each, against opponents they largely do not choose, and at the end a committee selects twelve of them for a playoff. The schedule graph is sparse: a team plays fewer than a tenth of the other teams in its division, most of them from its own conference, and conferences are linked by a few dozen non-conference games played in September. Any ranking has to propagate information about strength through that graph, and the history of the problem is largely the history of ways to do so: least squares on scoreboard margin [@harvilleUseLinearmodelMethodology1977; @masseyStatisticalModelsApplied1997], paired-comparison models for wins and losses [@bradleyRankAnalysisIncomplete1952; @measePenalizedMaximumLikelihood2003], eigenvector methods [@keenerPerronFrobeniusTheorem1993], and linear-algebraic record-only schemes such as the Colley matrix [@colleyColleysBiasFree2002], one of the computer components of the Bowl Championship Series era [@sternStatisticsCollegeFootball2004; @langvilleWhosNumberOne2012].

These methods disagree partly because they answer different questions. A *predictive* rating asks which team would win a game played next week, and by how much. Margin of victory is informative about that, so a predictive rating should use it, together with any other signal of how well a team played. A *retrodictive* ranking asks what a team has earned by its results. Here margin is usually excluded on purpose, so that a team is neither rewarded for running up a score nor penalised for resting its starters, and a win over a strong opponent is worth more than a win over a weak one. Combining the two into one number, as weighted composites of standardised scores do, gives a quantity that answers neither question and whose weights cannot be validated against anything observable.

This paper keeps the two apart but derives both from one posterior distribution. The contributions are four.

1. A **power model** (@sec-power) for team strength in points on a neutral field, observed through the regulation scoreboard margin and through an efficiency margin built from expected points added per play [@yurkoNflWARReproducibleMethod2019]. The margin is modelled *conditionally* on the efficiency residual, so the two signals share one latent strength without being treated as independent evidence, and their relative weight is estimated rather than set. Strength is pooled within conferences and within three divisional tiers, carried over from the two previous seasons by estimated coefficients, shifted before the season by roster information (returning production and recruited talent), and moves through the season as a random walk whose step size is estimated. The shape of the margin distribution is one of four families, chosen by cross-validation on every complete season (@sec-family); the published one is the `r fam_name[[fam]]`. A parallel model for the total score, observed through the final score and summed offensive efficiency, splits each rating into offence and defence without changing it (@sec-total).
2. A result on how much the efficiency signal adds (@sec-info). Under a Gaussian version of the model the gain in per-game Fisher information about strength has a closed form, and at the fitted parameters it is `r fmt(100 * min(info$gain), 1)`--`r fmt(100 * max(info$gain), 1)`\% --- small, and explained by the estimated scale of efficiency being close to the value at which the gain vanishes. An ablation backtest measures the same thing out of sample (@sec-ablation).
3. A **resume** measure, Wins Above Benchmark (@sec-resume): for each posterior draw, the number of wins a team has beyond those the draw's twelfth-best FBS team would be expected to earn against the same opponents at the same venues. It is additive over games, never rewards a loss, is centred at zero for a team exactly as strong as the benchmark, and inherits uncertainty in the opponents, the benchmark and the ranks directly from the posterior.
4. A **validation** of the whole system (@sec-computation, @sec-checks, @sec-backtest) on every week of every season from `r first_season` to `r current`: `r n_snap` weekly posteriors fitted by the No-U-Turn sampler, of which `r n_pass` pass the convergence gates; posterior predictive checks, which reproduce the spread, the blowouts and home-field advantage but miss the share of one-score games in `r n_w7_fail` of `r nrow(w7)` seasons; prior-sensitivity diagnostics, which flag `r n_flagged_any` of `r nrow(flag_counts)` structural parameters in at least one season; simulation-based calibration; ablations and baselines; and a rolling backtest of `r fmt(bt_all$games)` games, each predicted from the posterior fitted through the week before, scored against the result and the closing betting line.

@fig-overview shows how these pieces fit together. @sec-data describes the data, @sec-power and @sec-info the power model, and @sec-resume the resume and the reference rankings. @sec-computation describes fitting and the pipeline, @sec-checks model checking, @sec-backtest the out-of-sample evaluation, @sec-results the `r last_full` season as a worked example, and @sec-discussion the limitations.

::: {#fig-overview fig-scap="Structure of the paper"}

Structure of the paper. One posterior per week feeds both products; the dashed arrow is the only link between them: the Resume values results using opponent and benchmark strengths drawn from the Power posterior, but never uses margin. Each box names the section where it is developed.
:::

**Related work.** The margin model descends from @harvilleUseLinearmodelMethodology1977 and @harvillePredictionsNationalFootball1980, who fit mixed linear models to scoreboard margin with random team effects, and from @sternProbabilityWinningFootball1991, who showed that National Football League margins are close to normal around the betting line with a standard deviation near fourteen points, so that a spread determines a win probability. @glickmanStatespaceModelNational1998 made team strengths evolve over time in a Bayesian state-space model; the weekly random walk here is a version of theirs. Using the $t$ distribution for robustness to blowouts follows @langeRobustStatisticalModeling1989. On the retrodictive side, @measePenalizedMaximumLikelihood2003 and @colleyColleysBiasFree2002 give record-only rankings; @sternStatisticsCollegeFootball2004 discusses why the Bowl Championship Series excluded margin from its computer rankings, and @lopezHowOftenDoes2018 quantify how much of a season's outcome is noise, which is the reason a resume should report uncertainty. Dynamic paired-comparison models [@glickmanParameterEstimationLarge1999; @knorrheldDynamicRatingSports2000] let strengths drift between games, and @annisHybridPairedComparison2005 combine win--loss and margin information for college football specifically. Among published football ratings, Elo systems [@eloRatingChessplayersPast1978; @silverHowOurNFL2014] update a rating after each game, SP+ [@connellySPPrimer2023] and ESPN's FPI [@espnFPI2023] are proprietary efficiency-based power ratings, and Massey's composite [@masseyCompositeRankings2026] aggregates about a hundred computer rankings. Wins Above Benchmark is the football analogue of the "wins above bubble" measure on the team sheets of the college basketball selection committee [@ncaaNETTeamSheets2024], with the benchmark placed at the playoff boundary. The workflow follows @gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020.

## Notation {#sec-notation}

@tbl-notation collects the notation. Games are indexed by $g$, teams by $i$ and $j$, weeks by $w$, conferences by $c$ and divisional tiers by $\ell \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ for FBS, the Football Championship Subdivision (FCS) and all lower divisions. Game $g$ is played in week $w(g)$. Posterior draws are indexed by $s = 1, \ldots, S$, and a superscript $(s)$ marks a quantity evaluated at draw $s$. A team's rating without a week index, $r_i$, is its rating at the week of the snapshot being published. The code keeps its own variable names; @tbl-notation gives both, and the total model of @sec-total has its own, listed there.

# Data {#sec-data}

All data come from the CollegeFootballData.com API [@cfbd2026]: every game involving an FBS or FCS team from `r first_season` to `r current`, with line scores, venue, divisional classification and conference of each team; per-game advanced statistics; closing betting lines (the spread and the over/under); and the AP, Coaches and College Football Playoff (CFP) polls. Teams are keyed by the provider's identifiers throughout. The following derived quantities enter the model.

**Regulation margin.** $y_g$ is the home score minus the away score after four quarters, computed from the line scores. A game decided in overtime (`r pct(mean(games$ot, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` of games) therefore contributes a margin of zero. This is deliberate: overtime is a different game, with possession alternating from the opponent's 25-yard line, and its points say little about strength. The win still counts as a win in the resume.

**Efficiency margin.** For each side the provider reports the mean predicted points added (PPA) per play and the number of plays, both with garbage time excluded. PPA is the change in expected points across a play, where expected points are estimated from down, distance and field position [@yurkoNflWARReproducibleMethod2019]. We use the net total,
$$
e_g = \overline{\mathrm{PPA}}_{h(g)} \, n_{h(g)} - \overline{\mathrm{PPA}}_{a(g)} \, n_{a(g)},
$$
which is on the scale of points. It measures how well each offence moved the ball regardless of how drives ended, so it is less exposed than the scoreboard to turnovers returned for touchdowns, missed field goals and fourth-down variance. It is used only when both offences have at least `r cfg$min_plays` non-garbage plays, and is missing otherwise --- in practice for most games against lower-division opponents, which the provider does not chart.

**Total.** For the total model (@sec-total), $x_g$ is the final combined score and $e^+_g = \overline{\mathrm{PPA}}_{h(g)} \, n_{h(g)} + \overline{\mathrm{PPA}}_{a(g)} \, n_{a(g)}$ the summed offensive efficiency, available exactly when $e_g$ is. The total of a game decided in overtime is inflated by the extra possessions, so for those games $x_g$ is treated as missing and only $e^+_g$ is used.

**Preseason information.** Three quantities from before the season enter the preseason level of each FBS team (@sec-hierarchy): the share of last season's offensive production, measured in PPA, that returns (the provider's *returning production*); the 247Sports team talent composite, a recruiting-based measure of the roster [@cfbd2026], available from `r first_season + 1`; and the team's final rating two seasons back. Returning production is centred and the talent composite standardised within FBS each season; both are zero for FCS and lower-division teams, which the provider does not cover. A head-coach change was also built as a candidate input and not adopted (@sec-loso).

**Tiers and conferences.** Each team is assigned to FBS, FCS or a single pooled tier for Division II, III and NAIA opponents, and to its conference in that season. An independent is not a conference, so each independent (`r fmt(n_fbs_ind)` FBS programmes over the period, among them `r paste(head(fbs_ind, 4), collapse = ", ")`) gets a conference effect of its own, drawn from its tier like any conference's; the lower-division opponents share one.

**Missing efficiency.** The efficiency margin is missing for `r pct(1 - mean(!is.na(games$home_ppa) & !is.na(games$away_ppa)))` of games, almost all of them involving an FCS or lower-division team that the provider does not chart. Missingness therefore depends on the tiers of the two teams, which are observed, and not on how the game went, so the data are missing at random in the sense of @rubinInferenceMissingData1976 and the likelihood of the observed data (@eq-lik-marg for these games) is the right one to use without modelling why efficiency is missing.

**Weeks.** Postseason games are relabelled as one week after the last regular-season week. In the season being played, a week counts as concluded once at least 90\% of its games are final and six hours have passed since its last kickoff; in a finished season, every week with at least one result counts, since the remaining games were cancelled. Only a contiguous prefix of weeks can be concluded. A posterior fitted "through week $w$" uses exactly the games of concluded weeks $\le w$.

**The 2020 season.** The 2020 season was shortened and partly cancelled, and most FCS conferences moved their season to the spring of 2021. Those `r fmt(sum(grepl("spring", games$season_type)))` spring games belong to the 2020 season in the provider's data but are numbered from week 1 again; left as they are, a posterior "through week 3" of 2020 would contain games played five months later. They are therefore placed after the fall postseason in date order, as spring weeks 1 to `r max(games$week[games$season_type == "spring_regular"], na.rm = TRUE)` followed by a spring postseason, and fitted and backtested like any other weeks.

@tbl-data summarises the data.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-data
#| tbl-cap: "Completed games by season. FBS--FBS games carry most of the information about FBS strength; FBS--FCS games link the two tiers. \\emph{Eff.} is the share of games with an efficiency margin; \\emph{Snap.} is the number of weekly posteriors fitted, including the preseason one from 2015."
g <- games |>
  filter(completed, !is.na(home_points)) |>
  mutate(pair = paste(pmin(home_class, away_class), pmax(home_class, away_class)),
         has_eff = !is.na(home_ppa) & !is.na(away_ppa))
g |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(Games = n(), `FBS--FBS` = sum(pair == "fbs fbs"),
            `FBS--FCS` = sum(pair == "fbs fcs"), `FCS--FCS` = sum(pair == "fcs fcs"),
            Other = Games - `FBS--FBS` - `FBS--FCS` - `FCS--FCS`,
            Eff. = mean(has_eff), Neutral = mean(neutral_site), OT = mean(ot, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  left_join(params |> count(season, name = "Snap."), by = "season") |>
  mutate(across(c(Eff., Neutral, OT), \(x) pct(x)),
         across(c(Games:Other), \(x) fmt(x)),
         season = ifelse(season == current, paste0(season, "$^\\ast$"), season)) |>
  rename(Season = season) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrrrrr")
```

\vspace{-0.5em}
\qmdsmaller{$^\ast$ In progress: through week `r max(params$week[params$season == current])`.}

# The Power Model {#sec-power}

## Likelihood {#sec-likelihood}

For game $g$ let
$$
\mu_g = r_{h(g),w(g)} - r_{a(g),w(g)} + \eta\,\delta_g
$$
be the expected regulation margin: the difference between the two teams' strengths in the week of the game, plus the home-field advantage when the game is not at a neutral site. Both observed signals depend on the teams only through $\mu_g$. How strengths move from week to week is the subject of @sec-hierarchy.

::: {.defn label="Power model likelihood."}
For a game with an efficiency margin,
$$
e_g \mid \mu_g \sim \mathcal{N}\bigl(\lambda\mu_g,\ \sigma_e^2\bigr), \qquad
y_g \mid e_g, \mu_g \sim \mathcal{D}\bigl(\mu_g + \kappa(e_g - \lambda\mu_g),\ \sigma_m;\ \mu_g\bigr),
$$ {#eq-lik}
where $\mathcal{D}(\xi, \sigma; \mu)$ is a law with location $\xi$ and scale $\sigma$ from one of the four families of @tbl-families. For a game without one,
$$
y_g \mid \mu_g \sim \mathcal{D}\bigl(\mu_g,\ \bar\sigma;\ \mu_g\bigr), \qquad \bar\sigma^2 = \sigma_m^2 + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2,
$$ {#eq-lik-marg}
with the mixture's wide scale widened in the same way, $\bar\sigma_w^2 = \sigma_w^2 + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2$. Games are conditionally independent given the parameters.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-families
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("The four margin families. $t_\\nu(\\xi, \\sigma)$ is the Student-$t$ law with $\\nu$ degrees of freedom, location $\\xi$ and scale $\\sigma$. The published family, chosen by cross-validation (@sec-family), is the ", fam_name[[fam]], ".")'
tibble::tribble(
  ~Family, ~`$\\mathcal{D}(\\xi, \\sigma; \\mu)$`, ~`Extra parameters`,
  "Normal", "$\\mathcal{N}(\\xi, \\sigma^2)$", "none",
  "Student-$t$", "$t_\\nu(\\xi, \\sigma)$", "$\\nu$",
  "Scale mixture", "$(1 - p_w)\\,\\mathcal{N}(\\xi, \\sigma^2) + p_w\\,\\mathcal{N}(\\xi, \\sigma_w^2)$, $\\sigma_w > \\sigma$", "$p_w, \\sigma_w$",
  "Scale-$t$", "$t_\\nu\\bigl(\\xi, (\\sigma^2 + \\gamma^2\\mu^2)^{1/2}\\bigr)$", "$\\nu, \\gamma$"
) |>
  ktab(align = "lll")
```

Three features of @eq-lik matter. First, both signals load on the same $\mu_g$, so strength is measured in points of scoreboard margin: $\lambda$ converts it to the efficiency scale, and it is estimated. Second, the margin is modelled *given* the efficiency residual $e_g - \lambda\mu_g$. A team that outplays its expected efficiency usually outscores its expected margin too, and the loading $\kappa$ absorbs that shared component. Were the two modelled as conditionally independent given $\mu_g$, one good performance would be counted twice. Third, the margin is not normal. The Student-$t$ lets a 63--0 result inform strength without dominating it [@langeRobustStatisticalModeling1989]. The scale mixture puts most games in a narrow component and a minority in a wide one, which bunches margins near the expected value more than the $t$ does. The scale-$t$ lets the noise grow with the expected margin $|\mu_g|$: a mismatch is less predictable in size than an even game, because the favourite may empty its bench at any score. The family is a modelling choice made once, by leave-one-out cross-validation on every complete season (@sec-family), and its parameters are estimated in every fit.

The scale $\bar\sigma$ in @eq-lik-marg is chosen so that the two cases agree for the Gaussian families.

::: {.thm label="Marginal Margin Lemma."}
Replace $\mathcal{D}$ in @eq-lik by the normal law with the same location and scale. Then, marginally over $e_g$, $y_g \mid \mu_g \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_g, \bar\sigma^2)$, and $(e_g, y_g)$ is bivariate normal with mean $(\lambda\mu_g, \mu_g)$ and covariance
$$
\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_e^2 & \kappa\sigma_e^2 \\ \kappa\sigma_e^2 & \sigma_m^2 + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $e_g = \lambda\mu_g + \varepsilon_e$ and $y_g = \mu_g + \kappa\varepsilon_e + \varepsilon_m$ with $\varepsilon_e \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_e^2)$ and $\varepsilon_m \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_m^2)$ independent. Then $(e_g, y_g)$ is a linear image of a Gaussian vector, with the stated mean, $\Var(y_g) = \kappa^2\sigma_e^2 + \sigma_m^2$ and $\Cov(e_g, y_g) = \kappa\sigma_e^2$.
:::

The same argument applied to each component shows that @eq-lik-marg is exact for the normal and the scale mixture. Under the two $t$ families the marginal of $y_g$ is not exactly of the form @eq-lik-marg, so there it is an approximation that matches the location and the scale; it affects only the games without an efficiency margin, which are mostly lopsided games against lower-division teams. The same marginal law defines the predictive win probability. Write $F(\cdot \mid \mu)$ for the distribution function of $\mathcal{D}(\mu, \bar\sigma; \mu)$, the predictive law of a margin whose expected value is $\mu$.

::: {.defn label="Win probability."}
The probability that team $i$ beats team $j$ at venue $v \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ (away, neutral, home for $i$) is the posterior mean
$$
p_{ij}(v) = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S} \Bigl[1 - F^{(s)}\bigl(0 \bigm| \mu_{ij}^{(s)}(v)\bigr)\Bigr], \qquad \mu_{ij}^{(s)}(v) = r_i^{(s)} - r_j^{(s)} + \eta^{(s)} v,
$$
where $F^{(s)}$ uses the family's parameters in draw $s$. The predicted spread is the posterior mean of $\mu_{ij}(v)$.
:::

For the Student-$t$ family $1 - F(0 \mid \mu) = F_\nu(\mu/\bar\sigma)$, with $F_\nu$ the distribution function of the standard $t_\nu$ law: the rule of @sternProbabilityWinningFootball1991 with the normal replaced by the fitted $t$ and averaged over the posterior, which widens the predictive distribution by the uncertainty in the ratings. For the scale-$t$ it is $F_\nu\bigl(\mu/(\bar\sigma^2 + \gamma^2\mu^2)^{1/2}\bigr)$, which still increases with $\mu$ but approaches $F_\nu(1/\gamma)$ rather than one as $\mu$ grows: no favourite is certain. A game $h$ weeks after the snapshot adds the random-walk drift of both teams over those weeks (@sec-hierarchy) to $\mu_{ij}^{(s)}$ before the average is taken.

## Hierarchy, Preseason Information and the Weekly Walk {#sec-hierarchy}

A team's strength starts the season at a preseason level, pooled at two levels --- teams within conferences and conferences within tiers --- and then moves from week to week.

::: {.defn label="Strength hierarchy."}
For team $i$ in conference $c(i)$ of tier $\ell(i)$, the preseason (week-1) level is
$$
\begin{aligned}
r^0_i &= \alpha_{c(i)} + \beta_i\, d_i + \gamma_q\, q_i + \gamma_a\, a_i + \beta_2\, d^{(2)}_i + \bigl(\tau_{\ell(i)}^2 + \beta_i^2 s_i^2\bigr)^{1/2} z_i, \\
\beta_i &= \beta + \beta_q\, q_i, \qquad
\alpha_c = m_{\ell(c)} + \omega\, u_c, \qquad
z_i, u_c \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, 1),
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-hier}
with $m_1 = 0$. Here $d_i$ is team $i$'s final power rating in the previous season minus the mean final rating of its current tier, $s_i$ is the posterior standard deviation of that rating, and $d_i = s_i = 0$ when there is no previous rating (the first season, and teams new to the data); $d^{(2)}_i$ is the same deviation two seasons back. For FBS teams, $q_i$ is the share of last season's production that returns and $a_i$ the standardised talent composite (@sec-data), both zero for other teams and when missing. Returning production enters twice: as a level, $\gamma_q q_i$, and through the carry-over $\beta_i$, so that a team returning more of its roster may keep more of last season's deviation.
:::

::: {.defn label="Weekly random walk."}
Let $w_1 < w_2 < \cdots$ be the weeks in which team $i$ plays, and $w_0 = 1$. Its strength in those weeks is
$$
r_{i,w_k} = r_{i,w_{k-1}} + \phi_r\,(w_k - w_{k-1})^{1/2}\,\varepsilon_{i,k}, \qquad r_{i,w_0} = r^0_i, \qquad \varepsilon_{i,k} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, 1),
$$ {#eq-walk}
so a team that does not play in a week accumulates that week's variance at its next game. Its rating at the week $w$ of a snapshot is its last state plus the drift since, $r_i = r_{i,w_K} + \phi_r\,(w - w_K)^{1/2}\varepsilon_i$, with $w_K$ its last game week up to $w$.
:::

Only the weeks in which a team plays carry a state, so a season adds about a dozen parameters per team rather than one per week. The step $\phi_r$ is shared by all teams and estimated. It is the model's answer to how quickly a rating should forget: with $\phi_r = 0$ every game of the season counts equally, as in a static model, and the larger $\phi_r$ is relative to the noise of a game, the more the latest games dominate. A prediction for a game $h$ weeks after the snapshot adds independent drift for both teams, so the variance of the expected margin grows by $2h\phi_r^2$.

The parameterisation is non-centred [@papaspiliopoulosGeneralFrameworkParametrization2007] throughout, in $z_i$, $u_c$ and the steps $\varepsilon_{i,k}$: in early weeks each team has one or two games and the data barely constrain $z_i$, which is the regime in which a centred hierarchy produces the funnel geometry that defeats Hamiltonian samplers [@betancourtConceptualIntroductionHamiltonian2017]. The random walk has a funnel of its own, between $\phi_r$ and the steps, and the data identify $\phi_r$ only weakly, which is why its prior is informative and keeps it away from zero (@sec-priors).

The carry-over $\beta$ does most of the work of a preseason rating. In week 0 no game has been played and the posterior of $r_i$ is centred on $\beta_i d_i + \gamma_q q_i + \gamma_a a_i + \beta_2 d^{(2)}_i$ plus its conference and tier means; as games accumulate, the team effect $z_i$ and the steps take over. The roster terms and the second season back were each adopted because they improve out-of-sample predictions in the first weeks (@sec-loso). Because $d_i$ is measured against the tier and not the conference, it carries conference strength over as well, so preseason predictions of non-conference games are informative from the first week.

@fig-tau shows the estimated step by season. At the posterior mean of a typical complete season, $\phi_r = `r fmt(median(rw_s$tau[rw_s$season %in% complete]), 2)`$ points per week: over a twelve-week regular season a team's strength drifts by about $`r fmt(median(rw_s$tau[rw_s$season %in% complete]) * sqrt(12), 1)`$ points (one sd), small next to the spread of FBS strengths but not negligible next to the margin of a close game. Whether that drift improves predictions over static ratings is tested directly in @sec-ablation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tau
#| fig-cap: "Weekly random-walk step sd by season, posterior mean of the published final fit: $\\phi_r$ for strength and $\\phi_t$ for the total tendency of @sec-total. The dashed lines are the prior means."
#| fig-scap: "Random-walk step by season"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.32
rw_s |>
  filter(season %in% complete) |>
  pivot_longer(-season) |>
  mutate(name = factor(ifelse(name == "tau", "phi[r]~(strength)", "phi[t]~(total)"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(season, value)) +
  geom_hline(data = tibble(name = factor(c("phi[r]~(strength)", "phi[t]~(total)")),
                           pm = c(cfg$tau_r_prior[1], cfg$tau_t_prior[1])),
             aes(yintercept = pm), linetype = "dashed", colour = col_ref) +
  geom_point(colour = col_power, size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~name, labeller = label_parsed) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(first_season, last_full, 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Points per week")
```

**Uncertainty in last season's rating.** $d_i$ is built from a posterior mean, and last season's rating is itself uncertain: the final posterior standard deviation of an FBS rating is about `r fmt(median(di_rel$sd_med), 1)` points, against a spread of `r fmt(median(di_rel$sd_d), 0)` points in $d_i$. Treating the true previous rating as $\mathcal N(d_i, s_i^2)$ and integrating it out adds $\beta^2 s_i^2$ to the team's variance, which is the extra term in @eq-hier; a team whose previous rating was poorly determined is shrunk further towards its conference. Using the posterior mean as the covariate is regression calibration [@carrollMeasurementErrorNonlinear2006]: the posterior mean is already the best predictor of the true rating given last season's data, so the regression on it is not attenuated in the way a regression on a noisy measurement would be, and $\beta$ needs no correction. The reliability $1 - \bar s^2 / \Var(d)$ is `r fmt(min(di_rel$reliability), 2)`--`r fmt(max(di_rel$reliability), 2)` across seasons, so even a classical measurement-error correction would change $\beta$ by only a few percent.

**Teams that change tier.** A programme moving from FCS to FBS (`r fmt(nrow(movers))` team-seasons since `r first_season`, among them `r paste(head(unique(movers$team), 5), collapse = ", ")`) has a previous rating on the FBS scale far below the FBS mean, so its $d_i$ is strongly negative and its preseason rating keeps its absolute level rather than jumping to an average FBS team's. Its conference effect and $\tau_1$ are the new tier's. In weeks 1--4 of a transition season the out-of-sample error on these teams' FBS games is `r fmt(mover_err$mae[mover_err$mover], 1)` points (`r mover_err$games[mover_err$mover]` games), against `r fmt(mover_err$mae[!mover_err$mover], 1)` for other FBS games in the same weeks: larger, as expected for a team whose schedule changes completely, but not badly biased (mean error `r fmt(mover_err$bias[mover_err$mover], 1)` points).

**One conference spread for all tiers.** The team spreads $\tau_\ell$ differ by tier, but the conference spread $\omega$ is shared. FBS and FCS each have only about a dozen conferences a season, and the lower divisions are one node, so a tier-specific $\omega_\ell$ would be estimated from a dozen values and would lean on its prior. The fitted conference means support pooling: at the end of `r last_full` their standard deviation within FBS is `r fmt(conf_sd$sd[conf_sd$tier == 1], 1)` points and within FCS `r fmt(conf_sd$sd[conf_sd$tier == 2], 1)`.

**One home-field advantage.** $\eta$ is one number per season for every true home game, FBS or FCS, near or far. Travel, altitude and crowd size surely vary, but the data identify one average well and many small effects poorly. @fig-hfa shows the estimate by season: it is stable at about `r fmt(median(hfa_s$mean[hfa_s$season != 2020]), 1)` points, except in 2020, when most games were played without crowds and it falls to `r fmt(hfa_s$mean[hfa_s$season == 2020], 1)`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hfa
#| fig-cap: "Home-field advantage $\\eta$ by season: posterior mean and $\\pm 2$ sd of the full-season fit under vague priors (@sec-priors). The 2020 season was played largely without crowds."
#| fig-scap: "Home-field advantage by season"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.32
hfa_s |>
  ggplot(aes(season, mean)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = mean - 2 * sd, ymax = mean + 2 * sd), colour = col_ref, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(colour = col_power, size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = complete) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Home field (points)")
```

*Remark (identification).* The likelihood depends on the strengths only through differences $r_{i,w} - r_{j,w}$ within a connected component of the schedule graph, so it is flat along one direction per component. Every prior in the model is proper (@tbl-priors), so the posterior is proper regardless, and the published FBS-centred ratings $\tilde r_i = r_i - \bar r_{\text{FBS}}$ do not depend on the anchor $m_1 = 0$. Between components the relative strengths come from the prior alone --- from the carry-over and the tier and conference structure --- which is what happens in the first weeks.

@tbl-graph counts the components. In week 1 the FBS teams fall into dozens of pieces; the graph of teams that have played becomes connected within the FBS by week `r fmt(median(sg_first$first_connected[is.finite(sg_first$first_connected)]), 0)` in a typical season, and by the end of every season except `r paste(sg_final$season[sg_final$components > 1], collapse = " and ")` the whole graph, all three tiers, is one component. `r if (any(sg_final$components > 1)) paste0("In ", paste(sg_final$season[sg_final$components > 1], collapse = " and "), " a few teams (", paste(sg_final$components[sg_final$components > 1] - 1, collapse = ", "), " small component(s)) played only among themselves, and their ratings relative to everyone else rest on the prior.") else ""` @fig-graph draws one season's graph.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-graph
#| tbl-cap: "Connected components of the schedule graph among teams that have played, by season: after week 1, at the first snapshot in which all FBS teams are connected, and at the end of the season (all tiers)."
sg |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(`Week 1` = fbs_components[week == 1][1],
            `FBS connected from week` = min(week[!is.na(fbs_components) & fbs_components == 1]),
            `Final, all tiers` = components[week == max(week)], .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(Season = season) |>
  mutate(`Week 1` = paste(`Week 1`, "FBS"), `FBS connected from week` = ifelse(is.finite(`FBS connected from week`), `FBS connected from week`, NA)) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-graph
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("The ", last_full, " schedule graph, all completed games. Points are teams (FBS in orange, FCS in grey, lower divisions in light grey), placed by a force-directed layout so that conferences form clusters; lines are games. Non-conference games are the few long edges that tie the clusters together.")'
#| fig-scap: "The schedule graph"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.8
gg <- games |> filter(season == last_full, completed)
gr <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(data.frame(from = gg$home_id, to = gg$away_id), directed = FALSE)
set.seed(3)
lay <- igraph::layout_with_fr(gr, niter = 2000)
tier_of_id <- bind_rows(gg |> transmute(id = home_id, class = home_class), gg |> transmute(id = away_id, class = away_class)) |>
  distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE)
nodes <- tibble(id = as.integer(igraph::V(gr)$name), x = lay[, 1], y = lay[, 2]) |>
  left_join(tier_of_id, by = "id") |>
  mutate(tier = case_when(class %in% "fbs" ~ "FBS", class %in% "fcs" ~ "FCS", TRUE ~ "Lower"))
edges <- gg |> transmute(x = nodes$x[match(home_id, nodes$id)], y = nodes$y[match(home_id, nodes$id)],
                         xend = nodes$x[match(away_id, nodes$id)], yend = nodes$y[match(away_id, nodes$id)],
                         conf = conference_game)
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = edges, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend, alpha = conf), colour = "gray60", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x, y, colour = tier), size = 0.9) +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 0.35, `FALSE` = 0.8), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(FBS = col_power, FCS = "gray45", Lower = "gray75")) +
  theme_void(base_size = 10) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank())
```

Published ratings are the centred $\tilde r_i$, computed draw by draw, so a rating of $+10$ means ten points better than an average FBS team on a neutral field.

@fig-dag draws the full model as a directed acyclic graph.

::: {#fig-dag fig-scap="The power model as a graphical model"}

```{r}

cat(r"(\begin{tikzpicture}[
  lat/.style={draw, circle, minimum size=0.95cm, inner sep=0pt, font=\small},
  obs/.style={lat, fill=gray!20},
  par/.style={font=\small, inner sep=2pt},
  arr/.style={-{Stealth[length=1.8mm]}},
  plate/.style={draw, rounded corners=3pt, inner sep=6pt}]
% hyperparameters
\node[par] (m) at (0,0.2) {$m_\ell$};
\node[par] (om) at (1.6,0.2) {$\omega$};

\node[par] (beta) at (6.4,0.2) {$\beta$};

\draw[arr] (rw) -- node[right, font=\scriptsize, pos=0.35] {$h(g), a(g)$ in week $w(g)$} (mu);
\draw[arr] (del) -- (mu); \draw[arr] (eta) -- (mu);
\draw[arr] (mu) -- (e); \draw[arr] (mu) -- (y); \draw[arr] (e) -- (y);

\draw[arr] (lam.south) to[out=-35, in=-145] node[below, font=\scriptsize, pos=0.5] {$\lambda$; $\sigma_e$ via $\bar\sigma$ if $e_g$ missing} (y.south);

\node[plate, inner ysep=10pt, fit=(u)(al)] (pc) {};
\node[font=\scriptsize, anchor=south east] at (pc.south east) {conferences $c$};

```

The power model. Shaded nodes are observed; plates repeat over conferences, teams (and, for $\varepsilon_{i,k}$ and $r_{i,w}$, the weeks in which a team plays) and games; $s_i$, the posterior sd of $d_i$, enters $r^0_i$ alongside $d_i$ and is not drawn. "Family" stands for the shape parameters of the margin family ($\nu$, $\gamma$, or $p_w$ and $\sigma_w$). The total model of @sec-total has the same structure with its own parameters and is not drawn. The efficiency margin $e_g$ is a parent of the scoreboard margin $y_g$, which is how the conditional likelihood of @eq-lik avoids counting one performance twice. The curved edge carries two dependences: the residual $e_g - \lambda\mu_g$ enters $y_g$ through $\lambda$, and when $e_g$ is missing the edge $e_g \to y_g$ is marginalised as in @eq-lik-marg, so $\sigma_e$ enters $y_g$ through $\bar\sigma$.
:::

## Totals, Offence and Defence {#sec-total}

The margin says which team is better but not how many points a game will produce. A second latent quantity per team supplies that: a *total tendency* $t_{i,w}$, how far above or below the average the scores of team $i$'s games run. It has the same structure as strength --- a preseason level $t^0_i$ pooled within conferences (spread $\omega_t$) and tiers (offsets $m^t_2, m^t_3$), a within-conference spread $\tau^t$, a carry-over $\beta_t$ of last season's final total tendency measured against its tier, and a weekly random walk with its own step $\phi_t$ --- and is observed in the same way as strength, through a scoreboard quantity conditioned on an efficiency one.

::: {.defn label="Total model."}
With $T_g = t_{h(g),w(g)} + t_{a(g),w(g)}$, for a game with an efficiency margin
$$
e^+_g \mid T_g \sim \mathcal{N}\bigl(\alpha_s + \lambda_t T_g,\ \sigma_s^2\bigr), \qquad
x_g \mid e^+_g, T_g \sim \mathcal{N}\bigl(2\theta + T_g + \kappa_t(e^+_g - \alpha_s - \lambda_t T_g),\ \sigma_x^2\bigr),
$$ {#eq-total}
and for a game without one $x_g \mid T_g \sim \mathcal{N}(2\theta + T_g, \sigma_x^2 + \kappa_t^2\sigma_s^2)$. Here $\theta$ is the points each team scores in an average game.
:::

Strength and total tendency together give each team an offence and a defence. Writing $\mathrm{off}_i = (r_i + t_i)/2$ and $\mathrm{def}_i = (r_i - t_i)/2$, the expected scores of game $g$ are
$$
\text{home: } \theta + \tfrac{1}{2}(\mu_g + T_g), \qquad \text{away: } \theta + \tfrac{1}{2}(T_g - \mu_g),
$$
whose difference is the expected margin $\mu_g$ and whose sum is the expected total $2\theta + T_g$; the home-field advantage, part of $\mu_g$, adds $\eta/2$ to the home score and takes $\eta/2$ from the away score. The published **Off** and **Def** are the points a team would score and allow against an average FBS team on a neutral field, $\mathrm{Off}_i = \theta + \frac{1}{2}(\tilde r_i + t_i + \bar t)$ and $\mathrm{Def}_i = \theta + \frac{1}{2}(t_i + \bar t - \tilde r_i)$, with $\bar t$ the mean FBS total tendency, computed draw by draw. By construction $\mathrm{Off}_i - \mathrm{Def}_i = \tilde r_i$, the power rating.

The total model shares no parameter with the margin model of @eq-lik, and its likelihood involves only the total tendencies, so the joint posterior factorises: adding it changes neither the power rating nor the resume, only what is reported alongside them. The price of that separation is that the noise of the margin and the noise of the total are modelled as independent, and that overtime games inform the total only through $e^+_g$. The total is scored against the closing over/under in @sec-bt-accuracy.

## Priors {#sec-priors}

The structural parameters --- tier offsets, spreads, the carry-over and the preseason terms, home field, the likelihood scales, the random-walk steps and the total model --- describe the sport rather than any team. In the first weeks of a season, with about one game per team, the data cannot estimate them, and a vague prior leaves the sampler in a funnel. They are therefore given informative priors, set from history. Each complete season's final snapshot (about 1,550 games) is refitted under deliberately vague priors (@sec-supp-justify); the refits are the `prior_refits` target of the pipeline. The season-by-season posterior means $\hat\theta_s$, with posterior standard deviations $v_s$, are then pooled as in a random-effects meta-analysis. Each prior is centred at the weighted mean of the $\hat\theta_s$, with weights $w_s = 2^{-|s - s^\ast|/h}$ that halve every $h = `r cfg$pool$half_life`$ seasons away from the season $s^\ast$ the prior is for, and its standard deviation is the predictive standard deviation for a new season,
$$
\sigma_{\text{prior}}^2 = \max\bigl(\hat\sigma_b^2 - \bar v^2,\, 0\bigr) + \hat\sigma_b^2 / n_{\text{eff}},
$$ {#eq-pool}
where $\hat\sigma_b$ is the weighted between-season standard deviation of the $\hat\theta_s$, $\bar v^2$ the weighted mean of the $v_s^2$ and $n_{\text{eff}} = (\sum_s w_s)^2 / \sum_s w_s^2$. The first term is the season-to-season variation in excess of what estimation noise alone produces; the second is the uncertainty of the centre. The recency weights let the priors follow trends, such as the fall in scoring after the clock rules of 2023. An earlier version used equal weights and twice the between-season standard deviation, which counts estimation noise as variation and made the priors wider than the history supports; both choices were made on out-of-sample predictions of the first weeks (@sec-loso).

Two seasons are left out of the pooling. In `r first_season`, the first season of the data, there is no carry-over ($d_i = 0$ for every team), so the conference effects absorb team strength that later seasons attribute to $\beta d_i$, and $\omega$ is `r fmt(struct$mean[struct$variable == "sigma_conf" & struct$season == first_season], 1)` points against `r fmt(median(struct$mean[struct$variable == "sigma_conf" & struct$season != first_season]), 1)` in a typical later season; it measures a different quantity. And 2020, played largely without crowds, is left out for $\eta$ (@fig-hfa). @tbl-priors lists the priors with the range of the full-season posterior means under the vague priors and under the published priors.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-priors
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Priors (normal, truncated to the support where a parameter is constrained) and the range over complete seasons (", first_season, "--", last_full, ") of the full-season posterior mean, refitted under vague priors and as published. The last column is the median posterior sd of the vague-prior refits. The FBS tier offset is fixed at zero.")'
labs <- c(
  hfa = "$\\eta$ (home field)", b_prev = "$\\beta$ (carry-over)",
  lambda = "$\\lambda$", kappa = "$\\kappa$", sigma_eff = "$\\sigma_e$", sigma_m = "$\\sigma_m$",
  `mu_tier[2]` = "$m_2$ (FCS)", `mu_tier[3]` = "$m_3$ (lower)", sigma_conf = "$\\omega$",
  `sigma_team[1]` = "$\\tau_1$ (FBS)", `sigma_team[2]` = "$\\tau_2$ (FCS)", `sigma_team[3]` = "$\\tau_3$ (lower)"
)
pri <- tibble::tibble(
  variable = names(labs),
  mean = c(cfg$hfa_mean, cfg$b_prev_mean, cfg$lambda_prior[1], cfg$kappa_prior[1],
           cfg$sigma_eff_prior[1], cfg$sigma_m_prior[1], cfg$tier_mean, cfg$sigma_conf_prior[1],
           cfg$sigma_team_mean),
  sd = c(cfg$hfa_sd, cfg$b_prev_sd, cfg$lambda_prior[2], cfg$kappa_prior[2],
         cfg$sigma_eff_prior[2], cfg$sigma_m_prior[2], cfg$tier_sd, cfg$sigma_conf_prior[2],
         cfg$sigma_team_sd)
)
# Published final-week posterior means (params columns) under the published priors
pub_cols <- c(hfa = "hfa", b_prev = "b_prev", lambda = "lambda", kappa = "kappa", sigma_eff = "sigma_eff",
              sigma_m = "sigma_m", `mu_tier[2]` = "fcs_offset", `mu_tier[3]` = "nond1_offset",
              sigma_conf = "sigma_conf", `sigma_team[1]` = "sigma_team_fbs", `sigma_team[2]` = "sigma_team_fcs",
              `sigma_team[3]` = "sigma_team_nond1")
pub_final <- final_full |>
  select(season, all_of(unname(pub_cols))) |>
  pivot_longer(-season, names_to = "col") |>
  mutate(variable = names(pub_cols)[match(col, pub_cols)]) |>
  group_by(variable) |> summarise(plo = min(value), phi = max(value), .groups = "drop")
post <- struct |>
  filter(variable %in% names(labs)) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(lo = min(mean), hi = max(mean), psd = median(sd), .groups = "drop")
pri |>
  left_join(post, by = "variable") |>
  left_join(pub_final, by = "variable") |>
  transmute(Parameter = labs[variable],
            Prior = sprintf("$\\mathcal{N}(%s, %s^2)$", fmt(mean, 2), fmt(sd, 2)),
            `Vague priors` = sprintf("%s to %s", fmt(lo, 2), fmt(hi, 2)),
            `Published` = sprintf("%s to %s", fmt(plo, 2), fmt(phi, 2)),
            `Post.\\ sd` = fmt(psd, 2)) |>
  ktab(align = "llrrr")
noise_pars <- pooled |> filter(variable %in% names(labs), between_sd < 1.3 * typical_post_sd) |> pull(variable)
wide_pars <- pooled |> filter(variable %in% names(labs), between_sd >= 1.3 * typical_post_sd) |> pull(variable)
```

Some parameters vary between seasons and others hardly at all, and the table cannot distinguish real change from estimation noise by itself. Comparing the two standard deviations can: for `r length(noise_pars)` of the `r length(labs)` parameters (`r sym_list(noise_pars)`) the between-season standard deviation of the posterior means is less than 1.3 times the typical within-season posterior standard deviation, which is about what sampling noise alone would produce. For these the first term of @eq-pool vanishes and the prior standard deviation is the uncertainty of the centre alone: the history gives no evidence that the parameter changes from season to season.

The remaining parameters (@tbl-priors-other) are pooled in the same way. The degrees of freedom $\nu$ get the Gamma prior with the pooled mean and standard deviation, truncated to $\nu > `r cfg$nu_lower`$. The random-walk steps are refitted under a wide prior centred away from zero, $\phi_r \sim \mathcal N^+(0.8, 0.8^2)$ and $\phi_t \sim \mathcal N^+(1, 0.8^2)$: one with its mode at zero puts the sampler in the funnel between the step size and the steps (@sec-hierarchy). Before this version the refits kept the published step prior, $\phi_r \sim \mathcal N^+(0.6, 0.25^2)$; a season's posterior standard deviation of $\phi_r$ is about as large as that prior's, so pooling under it largely returned the prior. Under the wide prior the full-season estimates of $\phi_r$ range from `r fmt(min(struct$mean[struct$variable == "tau_r"]), 2)` to `r fmt(max(struct$mean[struct$variable == "tau_r"]), 2)` points per week. The total-model priors and the coefficients of the preseason terms are pooled likewise.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-priors-other
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Priors of the margin family, the random walk, the total model and the preseason terms, pooled from the refits like those of @tbl-priors: normal, truncated to the support where a parameter is constrained, unless stated. The last column is the range over complete seasons of the full-season posterior mean under the vague priors of @sec-supp-justify. Shape parameters of families other than the published ", fam_name[[fam]], " and preseason terms the published model does not use are omitted.")'
oth <- tibble::tribble(
  ~variable, ~what, ~mean, ~sd,
  "nu", "degrees of freedom", NA, NA,
  "gamma_m", "growth of the scale with $|\\mu|$", cfg$gamma_prior[1], cfg$gamma_prior[2],
  "p_wide", "weight of the wide component", NA, NA,
  "sigma_w", "wide scale (prior on $\\sigma_w - \\sigma_m$)", cfg$sigma_gap_prior[1], cfg$sigma_gap_prior[2],
  "tau_r", "weekly step of strength", cfg$tau_r_prior[1], cfg$tau_r_prior[2],
  "tau_t_raw[1]", "weekly step of the total tendency", cfg$tau_t_prior[1], cfg$tau_t_prior[2],
  "base_raw[1]", "points per team, average game", cfg$base_prior[1], cfg$base_prior[2],
  "t_tier_raw[1]", "FCS total offset", cfg$t_tier_mean[1], cfg$t_tier_sd[1],
  "t_tier_raw[2]", "lower-division total offset", cfg$t_tier_mean[2], cfg$t_tier_sd[2],
  "sigma_conf_t_raw[1]", "conference spread of totals", cfg$sigma_conf_t_prior[1], cfg$sigma_conf_t_prior[2],
  "sigma_t_team_raw[1]", "team spread of totals", cfg$sigma_t_team_prior[1], cfg$sigma_t_team_prior[2],
  "b_prev_t_raw[1]", "carry-over of totals", cfg$b_prev_t_prior[1], cfg$b_prev_t_prior[2],
  "lambda_t_raw[1]", "scale of summed efficiency", cfg$lambda_t_prior[1], cfg$lambda_t_prior[2],
  "alpha_es_raw[1]", "intercept of summed efficiency", cfg$alpha_es_prior[1], cfg$alpha_es_prior[2],
  "sigma_es_raw[1]", "noise of summed efficiency", cfg$sigma_es_prior[1], cfg$sigma_es_prior[2],
  "kappa_t_raw[1]", "loading of the total on it", cfg$kappa_t_prior[1], cfg$kappa_t_prior[2],
  "sigma_tot_raw[1]", "noise of the total", cfg$sigma_tot_prior[1], cfg$sigma_tot_prior[2],
  "b_ret_raw[1]", "carry-over per unit returning production", cfg$b_ret_prior[1], cfg$b_ret_prior[2],
  "c_ret_raw[1]", "level per unit returning production", cfg$c_ret_prior[1], cfg$c_ret_prior[2],
  "b_tal_raw[1]", "level per sd of talent", cfg$b_tal_prior[1], cfg$b_tal_prior[2],
  "b_prev2_raw[1]", "carry-over from two seasons back", cfg$b_prev2_prior[1], cfg$b_prev2_prior[2],
  "b_prev_low_raw[1]", "carry-over of lower tiers", cfg$b_prev_low_prior[1], cfg$b_prev_low_prior[2],
  "delta_coach_raw[1]", "log scale of $\\tau$ after a coaching change", cfg$delta_coach_prior[1], cfg$delta_coach_prior[2]
)
fam_vars <- switch(fam, normal = character(0), t = "nu", mixture = c("p_wide", "sigma_w"), scale_t = c("nu", "gamma_m"))
pre_on <- c(`b_ret_raw[1]` = isTRUE(cfg$use_ret), `c_ret_raw[1]` = isTRUE(cfg$use_ret), `b_tal_raw[1]` = isTRUE(cfg$use_tal),
            `b_prev2_raw[1]` = isTRUE(cfg$use_prev2), `b_prev_low_raw[1]` = isTRUE(cfg$b_prev_tier),
            `delta_coach_raw[1]` = isTRUE(cfg$use_coach))
oth |>
  filter(!variable %in% c("nu", "gamma_m", "p_wide", "sigma_w") | variable %in% fam_vars) |>
  filter(!variable %in% names(pre_on) | variable %in% names(pre_on)[pre_on]) |>
  left_join(struct |> group_by(variable) |> summarise(lo = min(mean), hi = max(mean), .groups = "drop"), by = "variable") |>
  transmute(Parameter = var_tex[variable], Meaning = what,
            Prior = case_when(
              variable == "nu" ~ sprintf("$\\mathrm{Gamma}(%s, %s)$, $\\nu > %s$", fmt(cfg$nu_prior[1], 1), fmt(cfg$nu_prior[2], 2), cfg$nu_lower),
              variable == "p_wide" ~ sprintf("$\\mathrm{Beta}(%s, %s)$", cfg$p_wide_prior[1], cfg$p_wide_prior[2]),
              TRUE ~ sprintf("$\\mathcal{N}(%s, %s^2)$", fmt(mean, 2), fmt(sd, 2))),
            `Vague-prior refits` = ifelse(is.na(lo), "--", sprintf("%s to %s", fmt(lo, 2), fmt(hi, 2)))) |>
  ktab(align = c("l", ">{\\raggedright\\arraybackslash}p{4.6cm}", "l", "l"))
```

The priors are empirical Bayes at the level of the sport, and two consequences need checking. First, a season's own data help set its prior, so saying that its posterior lies inside that prior would be circular. @sec-supp-justify therefore also builds, for each season, the prior pooled from the *other* seasons only, and asks whether the season's own estimate lies inside it. Second, the early-week backtest of @sec-backtest for, say, 2016 uses priors informed by later seasons. @sec-loso refits those weeks under leave-one-season-out priors and measures the difference. @sec-supp-induced gives the priors they induce on team strengths, win probabilities and margins, and @sec-supp-perturb refits the model under widened and shifted priors.

# What the Efficiency Signal Adds {#sec-info}

The efficiency margin is expensive --- it needs play-by-play data --- and a natural question is how much it sharpens the estimate of strength once the scoreboard is known. The Gaussian version of the model answers it in closed form.

::: {.thm label="Information Proposition."}
In the Gaussian model of the Marginal Margin Lemma, the Fisher information about $\mu_g$ carried by one game is
$$
\mathcal{I}_{y} = \frac{1}{\Sigma_{22}} = \frac{1}{\sigma_m^2 + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2}
$$
from the margin alone, and
$$
\mathcal{I}_{e,y} = \frac{\lambda^2}{\sigma_e^2} + \frac{(1 - \kappa\lambda)^2}{\sigma_m^2}
= \mathcal{I}_y + \frac{(\lambda - \lambda^\ast)^2}{\Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}^2/\Sigma_{22}},
\qquad \lambda^\ast = \frac{\Sigma_{12}}{\Sigma_{22}} = \frac{\kappa\sigma_e^2}{\sigma_m^2 + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2},
$$ {#eq-info}
from both signals. Hence $\mathcal{I}_{e,y} \ge \mathcal{I}_y$, with equality exactly when $\lambda = \lambda^\ast$.
:::

::: {.proof}
For a Gaussian vector with mean $\bm a\mu$ and known covariance $\Sigma$ the information about $\mu$ is $\bm a^\top\Sigma^{-1}\bm a$. With $\bm a = (\lambda, 1)^\top$, factor the joint density as $p(y)\,p(e \mid y)$: the margin contributes $1/\Sigma_{22}$, and $e \mid y$ is normal with mean $\lambda\mu + (\Sigma_{12}/\Sigma_{22})(y - \mu)$ and variance $\Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}^2/\Sigma_{22}$, whose derivative in $\mu$ is $\lambda - \lambda^\ast$. Adding the two informations gives the second form of @eq-info. The first form follows by factoring instead as $p(e)\,p(y \mid e)$: $e$ contributes $\lambda^2/\sigma_e^2$ and $y \mid e$ has mean $(1 - \kappa\lambda)\mu + \kappa e$ and variance $\sigma_m^2$.
:::

The proposition says that the efficiency margin helps exactly insofar as its scale $\lambda$ differs from $\lambda^\ast$, the slope of the regression of $e$ on $y$. If efficiency were nothing but a noisy copy of the scoreboard, its mean would move with $\mu$ exactly as the regression predicts from $y$, and it would add nothing.

```{r}
i25 <- info |> filter(season == last_full)
```

::: {.example}
At the end of `r last_full` the posterior means are $\lambda = `r fmt(i25$lambda, 3)`$, $\kappa = `r fmt(i25$kappa, 3)`$, $\sigma_e = `r fmt(i25$sigma_eff, 2)`$ and $\sigma_m = `r fmt(i25$sigma_m, 2)`$. The margin alone then has scale $\bar\sigma = (\sigma_m^2 + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2)^{1/2} = `r fmt(sqrt(i25$S22), 2)`$ points and carries $\mathcal I_y = 1/\bar\sigma^2 = `r fmt(1000 * i25$i_y, 2)` \times 10^{-3}$ per game. The slope at which efficiency would add nothing is $\lambda^\ast = \kappa\sigma_e^2/\bar\sigma^2 = `r fmt(i25$lambda_star, 3)`$, `r fmt(abs(i25$lambda - i25$lambda_star), 3)` from the fitted $\lambda$. The second term of @eq-info is $(\lambda - \lambda^\ast)^2/(\sigma_e^2 - \kappa^2\sigma_e^4/\bar\sigma^2) = `r fmt(1000 * (i25$i_joint - i25$i_y), 3)` \times 10^{-3}$, so both signals together carry $\mathcal I_{e,y} = `r fmt(1000 * i25$i_joint, 2)` \times 10^{-3}$: a gain of `r pct(i25$gain, 1)`, or about `r fmt(12 * i25$gain, 2)` extra games' worth of information over a twelve-game season.
:::

@tbl-info evaluates @eq-info at the posterior means of each complete season's final fit.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-info
#| tbl-cap: "Per-game Fisher information about the expected margin under the Gaussian model, at each season's final posterior means. $R^2$ is the share of the margin's variance explained by the efficiency residual, $\\kappa^2\\sigma_e^2/\\bar\\sigma^2$."
info |>
  transmute(Season = season, `$\\lambda$` = fmt(lambda, 3), `$\\lambda^\\ast$` = fmt(lambda_star, 3),
            `$R^2$` = fmt(r2, 2),
            `$10^3\\mathcal{I}_y$` = fmt(1000 * i_y, 2), `$10^3\\mathcal{I}_{e,y}$` = fmt(1000 * i_joint, 2),
            Gain = pct(gain, 1)) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrr")
```

The efficiency residual explains `r pct(min(info$r2))`--`r pct(max(info$r2))` of the margin's variance, so the two signals are strongly related, and the fitted $\lambda$ lies within about `r fmt(max(abs(info$lambda - info$lambda_star)), 2)` of $\lambda^\ast$. The per-game information gain is correspondingly small: `r pct(min(info$gain), 1)` to `r pct(max(info$gain), 1)`, about `r fmt(median(info$gain) * 12, 2)` games' worth over a twelve-game season. Three caveats limit how far this should be read. The calculation is Gaussian, while the published margin law is the `r fam_name[[fam]]``r if (has_nu) paste0(", with fitted $\\nu$ from ", fmt(min(info$nu), 0), " to ", fmt(max(info$nu), 0)) else ""``r if (fam == "scale_t") ", whose scale grows with the expected margin, so that $\\sigma_m$ is the scale of an even game and a lopsided one carries less information than the calculation assigns it" else ""`; under a heavy-tailed likelihood the efficiency residual also helps decide *which* large margins are outliers, which a Fisher-information calculation at the mean does not capture. It holds $\lambda$, $\kappa$ and the scales fixed, whereas in the fit they are estimated jointly with strength. And it is per game: it does not measure any robustness the efficiency margin brings to the early weeks. The backtest is the arbiter. @sec-ablation refits the model without the efficiency likelihood on every week of `r min(abl_seasons)`--`r max(abl_seasons)`: on the same `r fmt(abl_sum$games[abl_sum$variant == "Margin only"])` games, the margin-only model's mean absolute error is `r fmt(abl_d("Margin only", "err_abs")$diff, 2)` points (standard error `r fmt(abl_d("Margin only", "err_abs")$se, 2)`) `r ifelse(abl_d("Margin only", "err_abs")$diff > 0, "higher", "lower")` and its Brier score `r fmt(1000 * abl_d("Margin only", "brier")$diff, 1)` $\times 10^{-3}$ (se `r fmt(1000 * abl_d("Margin only", "brier")$se, 1)`) `r ifelse(abl_d("Margin only", "brier")$diff > 0, "higher", "lower")`. At each season's final posterior the expected log predictive density of the margin itself (@sec-loo) `r ifelse(median(loo_cmp$diff) > 0, "favours the full model", "favours the margin-only model")` by `r fmt(abs(median(loo_cmp$diff)), 0)` in a typical season (full minus margin-only : `r fmt(min(loo_cmp$diff), 0)` to `r fmt(max(loo_cmp$diff), 0)` across seasons, standard errors about `r fmt(median(loo_cmp$se), 0)`).

# The Resume {#sec-resume}

## Wins Above Benchmark {#sec-wab}

A resume should value results, not performances, and should value them relative to a standard that matters for selection. The playoff takes twelve teams, so the natural standard is the twelfth-best team.

::: {.defn label="Benchmark."}
In posterior draw $s$, the benchmark strength $B^{(s)}$ is the twelfth largest of the FBS strengths $\{r_i^{(s)} : \ell(i) = 1\}$.
:::

The benchmark is a strength, not a team: in different draws it is a different team, and its uncertainty is part of the posterior.

::: {.defn label="Wins Above Benchmark."}
Let team $i$ have played games $g \in G_i$, with result $W_g \in \{0, 1\}$ (overtime wins count), opponent $o(g)$ and venue $v_g \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ from $i$'s side. The probability that the benchmark would have won the same fixture is
$$
\pi_g^{(s)} = 1 - F^{(s)}\bigl(0 \bigm| B^{(s)} - r_{o(g)}^{(s)} + \eta^{(s)} v_g\bigr),
$$
the win probability of @sec-likelihood with the benchmark in team $i$'s place, and
$$
\WAB_i^{(s)} = \sum_{g \in G_i}\bigl(W_g - \pi_g^{(s)}\bigr).
$$ {#eq-wab}
The published value is the posterior mean $\WAB_i = S^{-1}\sum_s \WAB_i^{(s)}$ with an 80\% interval.
:::

@eq-wab uses the scoreboard only through $W_g$: margin enters the resume solely by having informed the strengths of the opponents and the benchmark. Both are taken at the week of the snapshot, not at the week of the game: an opponent is valued at what the posterior now believes it to be, so a win over a team that improves later in the season gains value as it does. With the random walk the two can differ, by about $\phi_r\,|w - w(g)|^{1/2}$ points in sd. The following properties are elementary but they are the reason for the choice.

::: {.thm label="WAB Properties."}
For every draw $s$:

(i) *Additivity.* $\WAB_i^{(s)}$ is a sum of per-game contributions $W_g - \pi_g^{(s)}$, each in $(-1, 1)$.
(ii) *Monotonicity.* A win contributes $1 - \pi_g^{(s)} > 0$ and a loss $-\pi_g^{(s)} < 0$; with the draw held fixed, changing any loss to a win raises $\WAB_i^{(s)}$ by exactly one, whatever the opponent.
(iii) *Schedule response.* The contribution of a win is increasing in the opponent's strength and that of a loss is increasing too (a loss to a strong team costs less), and both are decreasing in the venue $v_g$: road wins count for more than home wins.
(iv) *Calibration.* If the model is correct and team $i$ has strength $r_i^{(s)} = B^{(s)}$, then $\E[\WAB_i^{(s)} \mid \text{parameters}] = 0$ for every schedule.
:::

::: {.proof}
Parts (i) and (ii) are immediate from @eq-wab, since $0 < \pi_g^{(s)} < 1$. For (iii), $1 - F(0 \mid \mu)$ is increasing in $\mu$ for every family of @tbl-families (for the scale-$t$ because $\mu/(\bar\sigma^2 + \gamma^2\mu^2)^{1/2}$ is increasing), so $\pi_g^{(s)}$ is decreasing in $r_{o(g)}$ and increasing in $v_g$, and both contributions have the form $\text{const} - \pi_g^{(s)}$. For (iv), under the model $\Pr(W_g = 1) = 1 - F(0 \mid r_i - r_{o(g)} + \eta v_g) = \pi_g^{(s)}$ when $r_i = B^{(s)}$, so each term has expectation zero.
:::

Property (ii) holds draw by draw. The *published* $\WAB_i$ changes by a slightly different amount when a result flips, because the result is also data for the posterior: a win moves the opponent's strength down, and the benchmark with it, so the new draws differ from the old ones. @sec-leakage measures a related effect of the margin. Property (ii) excludes what the old composite resume did, rewarding a team for *playing* strong opponents regardless of result; (iii) is the precise sense in which the schedule is counted once; and (iv) gives the scale its meaning: a positive $\WAB$ is evidence of having done better than a bubble team would have with the same games. Summing over games makes $\WAB$ a count, not a rate, so a team that plays a thirteenth game can gain from it. That is intended: a conference championship game is a real opportunity to earn or lose standing.

```{r}
# A bubble team: the final resume rank closest to 12 with a full season, from the published per-game rows
gr_last <- snapshots$game_resume |> filter(season == last_full, week == max(fin_last$week))
bubble <- fin_last |> filter(resume_rank %in% 11:13) |> arrange(abs(resume_rank - 12)) |> slice(1)
bub_games <- gr_last |> filter(team_id == bubble$team_id) |>
  left_join(games |> filter(season == last_full) |>
              select(game_id, week_seq, week_label, home_id, away_id, home_team, away_team, home_points, away_points, neutral_site),
            by = "game_id") |>
  arrange(week_seq) |>
  mutate(home = home_id == bubble$team_id,
         opp = ifelse(home, away_team, home_team),
         venue = ifelse(neutral_site, "N", ifelse(home, "H", "A")),
         pf = ifelse(home, home_points, away_points), pa = ifelse(home, away_points, home_points),
         W = as.integer(pf > pa), cum = cumsum(wab_game))
sor_bub <- {
  p <- bub_games$p_bench; dist <- 1
  for (pi in p) dist <- c(dist * (1 - pi), 0) + c(0, dist * pi)
  list(dist = dist, sor = sum(dist[(sum(bub_games$W) + 1):length(dist)]))
}
```

::: {.example}
@tbl-wab-example works through $\WAB$ for `r bubble$team`, `r bubble$wins`--`r bubble$losses` and ranked `r bubble$resume_rank` in the final `r last_full` resume. For each game, $\bar\pi_g$ is the posterior mean probability that the benchmark would have won the same fixture at the same venue; the contribution is $W_g - \bar\pi_g$, and the published $\WAB$ is their sum, `r fmt(sum(bub_games$wab_game), 2)`. (The mean of the per-draw sums equals the sum of the per-game means, so the table reproduces the published value exactly.) The strength of record of @sec-sor is the probability that a benchmark team with these independent chances wins at least `r sum(bub_games$W)` of the `r nrow(bub_games)` games; the Poisson-binomial recursion over the column $\bar\pi_g$ gives `r fmt(sor_bub$sor, 3)`.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-wab-example
```
